speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It seeks to prevent and suppress nuclear terrorism by specifically criminalising such acts and providing for international assistance in relation to such acts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The possibility of a nuclear terrorist attack in Southeast Asia is remote.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Regional terrorist elements are not known to have the capability to build nuclear devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They are also more likely to use conventional improvised explosive devices, which they are more familiar with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, the rise of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS) has heightened the global threat of terrorism using nuclear or radioactive devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 2015, ISIS announced in its English language magazine "Dabiq" that it intended to attack the United States (US) with either a nuclear device or explosives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Given its access to funding and a global network of supporters, it could conceivably build a crude improvised nuclear device.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As such, we cannot discount the possibility of ISIS or its supporters getting hold of nuclear material to carry out a terror attack whether against us or other countries, especially when many countries, including those in our region, use nuclear energy or are actively exploring the use of nuclear energy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In February this year, Malaysian authorities arrested eight people connected to the theft of Iridium-192, which is a radioactive material which can be used to make dirty bombs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In such instances, the perpetrator will face the mandatory death penalty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In any other case, he will receive life imprisonment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As required by the Convention, the Bill also criminalises other acts which can lead to the intentional and unlawful use of radioactive material or nuclear explosive devices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These include the intentional and unlawful possession of any radioactive material or nuclear explosive device and the making of a nuclear explosive device, with the intention to use such material or device to cause death, serious bodily injury, or substantial damage to property or the environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Any person outside Singapore who commits an act which constitutes a nuclear terrorism offence if carried out in Singapore is deemed to have committed the act here.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If taken into custody, the person would be charged, tried and punished accordingly in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This provision allows us to prosecute the offender in Singapore, if it is not possible or desirable to extradite him.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It ensures that perpetrators do not escape punishment, regardless of which country they are from, and where they committed these offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This approach is similar to that in other terrorism-related laws, such as the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Clause 13 includes provisions to facilitate extradition requests by countries which are parties to the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Every nuclear terrorism offence will be deemed as an extraditable crime for the purposes of Parts III and IV of the Extradition Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Convention also requires that state parties provide mutual legal assistance to other states parties, and Singapore will render assistance within our domestic legal framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It reiterates our commitment to combat terrorism, as a responsible member of the international community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Author Van Hipp describes this very well in his book "The New Terrorism".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It has taken on a completely new fate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Even as we do not house large-scale nuclear plants and facilities, being open to the world still puts us at a potential risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Advances in information technology (IT) and the availability of the radioactive materials have also increased the likelihood of all these attacks happening anywhere in the world, practically, in fact, made even a lot easier these days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some of these devices, when detonated and released, can disperse the radioactive materials over a wide area, contaminating persons, environment and property with long-lasting effects and impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These days, terrorists use hybrid models, that is, blending nuclear and conventional devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They may not be big but they are significant enough for us to be concerned about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, my queries include, firstly, does the Ministry have a listing of such facilities and industries in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, have there ever been any breaches thus far in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, how about our control at our borders?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are our detection strategies for deployment of border monitoring equipment and counters?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fifth, have there ever been any threat of this nature in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is an important commitment as a member of the global community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do we have sufficient numbers of persons and expertise trained in this area to contribute significantly and meaningfully?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Seven, being a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and also being a strong advocate of nuclear non-proliferation and arms control, Singapore's stand is very clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If in the event of an occurrence of such an incident, how does Singapore share on the international platform and database?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How is Singapore planning and training for this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do we subscribe to any such databases, for example, the Johnston Archive or The Global Chronology?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In 1996, the International Court of Justice delivered their now famous advisory opinion to a controversial question.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They were asked whether the threat or use of nuclear weapons in any circumstances is permitted under international law.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The late great Judge Christopher Weeramantry was one of the seven dissenting Judges in the 1996 International Court of Justice (ICJ) Case, and he said that the "use of nuclear weapons contradicts the fundamental principle of the dignity and worth of the human person upon which all law must depend.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It endangers the human environment in a manner which threatens the entirety of life on this planet".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, that same year, in 1996, the United Nations (UN) Secretary-General at that time, after his review of the applicable international law, concluded that there was a need to elaborate on international treaties, including on a treaty preventing the use of weapons of mass destruction by terrorists.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: After several rounds of treaty drafting and negotiations, the International Convention for the Suppression of Nuclear Terrorism was opened for signature in April 2005.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Convention does not impose any new obligations on states in their use of nuclear weapons.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It covers primarily the activities by nuclear terrorists, to be exact.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It requires states to criminalise these offences via national legislation and to establish penalties in line with the gravity of such crimes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, high time for this Bill, Madam.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This House should welcome the basis for jurisdiction that this Bill sets out, which is a version of universal jurisdiction or tri-extradite, its guidelines for extraditions, the punitive measures it puts in place, and other measures it seeks to enact to prevent, deter and counter nuclear terrorism which takes place inside or outside Singapore's territorial borders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: For the sake of clarity, Madam, I would like to ask only the following questions of the Ministry.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The first and perhaps the most important question is: why did we wait so long?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the more pertinent question is: what is prompting our move this year to look at ratification?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister mentioned ISIS and, certainly, that must be a concern.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But are there issues or concerns closer to home, in this region, geopolitical threats that we may or should be concerned about?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, to what extent was the Ministry's desire to pass this Bill and to ratify the Convention, prompted by the US doing the same in 2015?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Third, going forward, how does the Ministry intend to cooperate with IAEA and the neighbouring Asian state parties which have also recently ratified this convention?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, I am thinking about South Korea, Indonesia and Vietnam, which have ratified this convention in the past two to three years.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: How would we be working with them to secure compliance?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What are the reasons for this particular provision in clause 14?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will other existing Government agencies potentially have a role in investigation and prosecution of Convention offences under this Bill and, if so, which agencies would these be?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that "a global regime of security which makes safety the result of terror and can speak of survival and annihilation as twin alternatives makes peace and the human future dependent upon terror.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a basis for world order".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: On that cautionary note, Madam, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill strengthens Singapore's position alongside other countries in the international fight against terrorism, in particular, nuclear terrorism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will be making some suggestions and raising two areas for clarification on the proposed provisions, as well as concerns on Singapore's efforts in combating terror threats involving chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive (CBRNE) materials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this limb is missing from section 4(b) and section 5(b) on possession and manufacture and I would like to seek clarification on this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is plausible that a person's intention in the possession or manufacture of these devices is not to cause death or injury to persons or damage to property or environment, but instead to compel individuals and governments to act in certain ways.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, in the October 2001 US anthrax attacks, letters containing anthrax spores were mailed to reporters and political figures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The intention of the senior scientist at the US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases who did so was not to kill or sicken anyone, but to enhance the proﬁle of his anthrax work, to improve his own standing among colleagues and to stimulate funding for biodefense by inducing fear in the population and influencing government policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the proposed section 9 makes it an offence to demand another person to make available to the offender or to give the offender access to any radioactive material, Convention device, or nuclear facility.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is only an offence if the demand is made by the use of force or by threats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is conceivable that these individuals may induce others to act through the promise of reward or gratification.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also note that section 11 outlines the extraterritorial nature of nuclear terrorism offences, stating that any person outside of Singapore committing an act which "if committed in Singapore, would constitute a nuclear terrorism offence", would be deemed to have contravened the law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will help to bring our legislative regime in line with international law on nuclear terrorism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nuclear terrorism is but one of the elements of CBRNE threats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addressing other aspects of CBRNE threats, Singapore has signed and ratified the Biological Weapons Convention and the Chemical Weapons Convention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Domestically, the Chemical Weapons (Prohibition) Act, Biological Agents and Toxins Act, and Strategic Goods (Control) Act are some of the pieces of legislation passed to prevent access of non-state actors to CBRNE materials and to criminalise abuse of these hazardous materials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Whilst strengthening our legislative framework, are we also doing enough to address security risks for facilities that hold dual-use materials which could be exploited or repurposed for terrorist usage?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Although Singapore does not have significant nuclear material or facilities, it is relatively easy to weaponise chemical, biological, radiological or explosive materials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All cases of theft of nuclear materials that have occurred overseas where the circumstances of the theft are known were perpetrated either by insiders or with the help of insiders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A nuclear or radioactive explosion will claim many lives or severe damage to property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nuclear or radioactive contamination will have serious health and environmental consequences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The affected areas would require extensive cleaning up before they are safe to live in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, we cannot rule out the possibility of such a terrorist attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the years, we have been preparing and developing capabilities to deal with such risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked what reasons prompted us to seek ratification now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After signing on to the Convention in 2006, we conducted detailed studies of the capabilities required to meet the Convention's requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since then, agencies, such as the National Environment Agency (NEA) and Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) have developed the necessary operational capabilities to deal with the illicit use of nuclear and radioactive materials in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and NEA have also been working together to tighten the security measures at the premises of licensees that are storing higher risk radioactive materials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also have to bear in mind that we are operating in a framework of various criminal legislation, such as the Radioactive Protection Act, which includes clauses, such as in Part VIIIA of the 	Radiation Protection Act (RPA) that relates also to the misuse of nuclear material.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also have the Penal Code and other legislation, basically those that pertain to terrorist acts, such as the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act and Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Altogether, the framework of laws provides an umbrella of legislation to counter and deal with acts of terrorism, whether they are in the preparatory stage, advanced in the operations or even the actual act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked what measures are in place to prevent a nuclear terrorist attack in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we have a strict regulatory regime in place to make it hard for radioactive material in Singapore to end up in the wrong hands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All local entities that possess or deal in radioactive material are licensed by NEA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These activities are regulated under the Radiation Protection Act and its subsidiary regulations, which take reference from the IAEA guidelines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NEA has also worked with the security agencies to tighten security measures at radioactive material storage sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the import of radioactive material, valid permits are required for all cargo entering our port checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If necessary, the cargo will be subject to x-ray screening and radioactivity checks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Any radioactive material detected is verified against the permits, and must comply with permit conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we will be cooperating with IAEA and other regional State Parties, and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singapore is a participating State of the IAEA's Incident and Trafficking Database (ITDB).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries are also strengthening cooperation on nuclear issues through the ASEAN Network of Regulatory Bodies on Atomic Energy (ASEANTOM).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ASEANTOM is working closely with IAEA to support the establishment of a regional environmental radioactivity database and an emergency preparedness and response framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked what measures we have in place to prepare for and deal with an attack.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we have established an interagency committee to oversee nuclear safety and security in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The committee continually assesses the threat of nuclear terrorism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Agencies validate existing plans and identify gaps through plan reviews and exercises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Interagency working groups undertake capability development to address the gaps and ensure agencies build up the necessary operational capabilities, facilities and measures to deal with these threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng mentioned the threat from other types of materials, such as biological and chemical materials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We would like to assure the Member that there are also interagency committees looking at the biological and chemical threats posed to Singapore, with similar structures and processes to continually review the protective security requirements for facilities that may contain such materials and our measures to deal with such threats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, our agencies have developed capabilities and processes to deal with possible threat scenarios, such as the detonation of a radiological dispersive device.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Should such an incident occur, MHA will coordinate a whole-of-Government response.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NEA will provide technical advice to the response agencies to help mitigate the harm from the radioactive materials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police will take the lead in investigating these terrorism acts to find the perpetrators and take them to task.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Police will work closely with other agencies where necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When hazardous materials, such as radioactive substances, are released into the environment, the authorities may have to evacuate people from the affected areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members of public may also be directed to initiate In-Place-Protection (IPP) at their homes or workplaces to reduce the risk of inhaling radioactive particles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This may include, for example, closing and sealing off gaps around all doors, windows and openings, and switching off all ventilation and air-con units that draw in air from the outside, until such time as the threat has dissipated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SCDF trains members of the public on how to conduct IPP as part of its Community Emergency Preparedness Programme (CEPP).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Participants will be briefed on the IPP procedures and have a hands-on session where they can practise on training simulators.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: IPP procedures are also included in the Civil Defence (CD) Emergency Handbook which is available for download on SCDF's website.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Should any member of the public come across any suspected illegal possession or use of radioactive material, or any attempts to make any radiological device, he should inform the Police immediately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested expanding the offences in the Bill to include other activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said earlier, the objective of the Bill is to ratify the Convention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The acts that are criminalised in the Bill, therefore, follow those set out in the Convention.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the two acts referred to by Mr Louis Ng, these are covered under existing legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the Member mentioned the scenario where a person may seek to gain access to material not by force but by unlawfully inducing others through the promise of reward or gratification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Depending on the actual circumstances, this could be an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act, among other offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similarly, the possession or manufacture of any radioactive material without a licence, regardless of intent, is an offence under RPA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to monitor the types of terrorist attacks or activities carried out and consider in future if there is a need to further amend the laws.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a consistent approach for other terrorism-related offences, such as those in the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng also had questions on the extraterritorial jurisdiction of offences under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had spoken about this in the opening speech.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The scope of extraterritorial jurisdiction in the Bill is similar to that in other terrorism-related offences, again, such as the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act and others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are no immediate threats, but we take the possibility seriously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is timely that we put in place the necessary legal framework now and join the international community to combat terrorism in all its forms, including nuclear terrorism.
